title: Imitate God (Jeremiah 9:23)
hookLine: the Guide ends: know God, then practice kindness, justice and righteousness

cards: The final chapter of a long, difficult book. Maimonides has spent the whole Guide for the Perplexed on hard questions: what words about God can mean, how prophecy works, why the commandments exist.

A reader might expect one last proof, sealed and abstract. Instead he sorts out what people chase in life, opens the book of Jeremiah, and lands on three plain Hebrew words: kindness, justice, righteousness.
A whole philosophy ends at the door of an ordinary deed.

teach.b: Imitate God. First, four things people call perfection. Maimonides lists them in order: what you own, the health and strength of your body, good character, and true knowledge of God.

Possessions can be gone overnight, he says, and were never really part of you. A strong body is something an animal has too. Good character is precious, but it mostly matters in how you deal with other people.
Knowledge of God is the one that is truly your own.
Second, Jeremiah seems to agree: "Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom," nor the mighty in his might, nor the rich in his riches. Glory instead in understanding and knowing God.
So far the mind sounds like the finish line. Third, the verse keeps going.

Jeremiah says what kind of God: the LORD who does mercy, justice and righteousness in the earth, "for in these things I delight, saith the LORD." In Hebrew, chesed, mishpat, tzedakah. Maimonides slows down here.
The goal, he says, is to know God's ways, and whoever comes to know them will set out to act the same way. Fourth, this is a commandment, not only an ideal.
In his law code he counts it from Deuteronomy, "and walk in His ways," with the rabbis' explanation: as God is called gracious, be gracious; as God is called merciful, be merciful.

teach.h: FOR IN THESE THINGS I DELIGHT.
teach.b: So a book written for a perplexed student ends with a person getting up to do one kind thing.

how: Jewish teaching often links knowing God with walking in God's ways, and some communities study the Guide's last chapter alongside acts of kindness, justice and charity in daily life.

games.q: you've reached the Guide's last chapter. knowing God is the highest perfection. what does Maimonides say comes after it?
o: acting in God's ways: kindness, justice, righteousness.
leaving the world to study alone.
games.why: he reads Jeremiah to the end of the verse: the God worth knowing does mercy, justice and righteousness, and the one who knows will act the same way.

practice: Bring to mind the people you'll see in the next day, and find one who could use something small: a ride, a message, a meal, a fair hearing, an apology you owe.
Don't pick the grandest thing; pick the one you would actually do, and see yourself doing it, start to finish. If you pray, you can hold the words "and walk in His ways" for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Imitate God. The Guide's ending: come to know God's ways, then act in them, with kindness, justice and righteousness. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: and you shall walk in His ways (Deuteronomy 28:9), the commandment to imitate God.

carryVoice: Your line: knowledge leads to kindness. Rest well, and I'll see you tomorrow.
